paragraphs: Domain generalization asks a model to work on a target domain whose data are unavailable during training. This creates two connected difficulties: the target may differ from the training domains, and the model cannot directly assess those differences. The paper addresses both through a probabilistic framework that represents uncertainty in neural network weights.

The method combines variational Bayesian inference with a probabilistic formulation of domain invariance. It jointly develops representations and classifiers intended to remain useful across domains, implementing both within a two-layer Bayesian neural network. This makes uncertainty part of learning both how inputs are represented and how predictions are made.

Experiments cover four cross-domain visual recognition benchmarks, with state-of-the-art mean accuracy reported on each. Ablation studies support a synergistic benefit from applying the Bayesian treatment to representations and classifiers together. These findings provide empirical support for jointly modeling uncertainty and domain invariance when learning without access to target-domain data.
icml-2021-a-bit-more-bayesian-domain-inv.tldr: A Bayesian framework jointly learns domain-invariant representations and classifiers, achieving strong visual recognition results without target-domain training data.

paragraphs: Biological sequence models often begin with multiple sequence alignment, a preprocessing step that arranges sequences for comparison. The paper shows that this familiar workflow can create statistical problems when training generative probabilistic models for sequence prediction and forecasting. Its focus is therefore on how observed sequences enter the model, rather than only on the model's predictive machinery.

The proposed MuE distribution replaces alignment preprocessing with a structured observation distribution. This gives generative models a principled alternative for handling sequence structure. The authors prove that MuE generalizes popular biological alignment methods and precisely characterize how those methods differ from latent alignment models used in natural language.

Across several datasets, models using MuE outperform comparable methods in the reported experiments. The paper also applies them to forecasting pathogen evolution, presented as a new application for generative probabilistic sequence models. Together, the theoretical and empirical results support integrating alignment-related structure into probabilistic modeling when the goal is to predict future or unseen sequences.
icml-2021-a-structured-observation-distr.tldr: MuE replaces biological sequence alignment preprocessing with a structured probabilistic observation model that improves prediction and supports pathogen-evolution forecasting.

paragraphs: Online learning requires decisions as data arrive, including decisions about the learning system's own configuration. ChaCha addresses this problem by choosing hyperparameters during the online learning process. It organizes the search around a current champion and a changing group of live challengers, making configuration selection an ongoing part of learning.

The algorithm determines which configuration should be champion and schedules challengers using sample complexity bounds. These bounds inform how candidates are evaluated over time. An application-dependent oracle proposes configurations based on the champions, so the candidate-generation mechanism is an explicit part of the setup rather than something the algorithm's guarantee makes unnecessary.

The theoretical result guarantees sublinear regret after the optimal configuration enters consideration through that oracle. This means the cumulative performance gap grows more slowly than the learning duration under the stated condition. Experiments report good performance across a wide range of datasets while optimizing both feature-construction choices and hyperparameters, supporting the practical usefulness of the champion–challenger organization.
icml-2021-chacha-for-online-automl-bbe37.tldr: ChaCha manages competing online learning configurations and guarantees sublinear regret once an application-dependent oracle introduces the optimal configuration.

paragraphs: Incorrect training labels can misdirect a classifier. Class2Simi investigates whether changing the form of supervision can make this problem easier to handle. It converts individually labeled examples into pairs whose labels indicate whether the two examples share a class label, shifting the learning signal from class membership to similarity.

The paper provides a theoretical guarantee that this transformation reduces the noise rate, making the resulting noisy similarity labels easier to handle in principle. It also shows that a deep network can learn to predict clean class labels from these pairs when it is first pretrained on the original noisy individual examples. That pretraining condition is part of the stated approach.

The conversion happens inside mini-batches as training proceeds, and the main computational change is to calculate the loss pairwise from model predictions. This keeps the framework computationally efficient. Extensive experiments support its effectiveness, suggesting that reformulating supervision can complement efforts to learn reliably from imperfect labels.
icml-2021-class2simi-a-noise-reduction-p.tldr: Class2Simi reduces label noise by converting class-labeled examples into similarity-labeled pairs and uses them to train classifiers after noisy-label pretraining.

paragraphs: An inverse problem asks what underlying signal could have produced a set of observations. This paper seeks a distribution over possible signals conditioned on those observations. It starts with a pretrained normalizing flow that models signals without conditioning, then treats reconstruction as conditional inference within that existing model.

The authors first establish that this inference problem is computationally hard for a large class of flow models. They respond with an approximate method that represents the desired conditional distribution by composing two flows. The resulting formulation supports a stable variational inference training procedure and does not require adversarial training.

Evaluations across several inverse problems produce high-quality samples together with uncertainty quantification. This matters because a distribution can represent multiple plausible reconstructions and the uncertainty associated with them. The paper also demonstrates amortization for zero-shot inference: the learned inference procedure can be reused to obtain conditional results. The contribution connects an expressive pretrained signal model with a practical approximation to its difficult conditional inference problem.
icml-2021-composing-normalizing-flows-fo.tldr: Composing two normalizing flows enables approximate conditional inference for inverse problems, producing plausible reconstructions with uncertainty estimates.

paragraphs: Conjugate energy-based models, or CEBMs, learn a joint probability model of observed data and hidden variables. Their central structural choice separates an intractable distribution over the data from a tractable posterior over the hidden variables. Thus, difficulty in handling the data distribution does not prevent tractable inference of latent variables from an observation.

Like variational autoencoders, these models can learn an unsupervised mapping from data into a latent representation. CEBMs omit a generator network, which the paper argues allows more flexible notions of similarity between observations. The representation can therefore serve familiar latent-variable modeling purposes while arising from a different model structure.

Experiments assess image modeling, the predictive usefulness of the latent space, and detection of data from outside the modeled domain. CEBMs achieve competitive results across multiple datasets on these measures. The findings support this combination of tractable latent inference and energy-based data modeling as a useful way to learn representations, without claiming that the full data distribution becomes tractable.
icml-2021-conjugate-energy-based-models-.tldr: CEBMs combine energy-based data modeling with tractable latent-variable inference, learning useful representations without a generator network.

paragraphs: Option learning organizes behavior through higher-level choices that can structure actions over time. Hindsight Off-policy Options, or HO2, learns these choices from trajectories by inferring which options were likely responsible for the observed behavior. It uses dynamic programming for this inference and backpropagates through that procedure to train all policy components together.

Because training is off-policy, the method can learn from trajectories beyond those produced by the policy currently being optimized. The paper reports that HO2 outperforms existing option-learning methods on common benchmarks. It also compares against flat policies and mixture policies with comparable optimization, helping distinguish the contribution of temporal abstraction from that of action abstraction.

The ablations highlight the importance of both forms of abstraction, alongside off-policy training and trust-region constraints. These effects are especially relevant in challenging simulated 3D robot manipulation tasks using raw pixel inputs. Finally, the authors modify the inference step to investigate stronger temporal abstraction, considering both training with pretrained options and learning from scratch.
icml-2021-data-efficient-hindsight-off-p.tldr: HO2 infers likely options from trajectories and differentiates through that inference to learn hierarchical policies efficiently from off-policy data.

paragraphs: Transformers need a useful way to divide their input into tokens. Video makes this difficult because its visual content is large and lacks an obvious counterpart to words. The ObjectCentric Video Transformer, or OCVT, addresses this by decomposing scenes into objects and using those objects as tokens for generative video modeling.

The model learns without supervision and captures spatial and temporal dynamics among multiple interacting objects. It uses these learned dynamics to generate future video frames. Factoring scenes into objects also reduces memory requirements relative to pixel-based models; the authors report training on sequences up to 70 frames long using one 48GB GPU.

Comparisons include previous recurrent-network approaches and alternative video-transformer baselines. OCVT performs well in the reported future-frame generation evaluations. Its learned representations also prove useful for video reasoning, achieving state-of-the-art performance on CATER. These findings support object-based tokenization as a way to address both computational demands and the need for representations that capture interactions within a scene.
icml-2021-generative-video-transformer-c.tldr: OCVT uses objects as video tokens to learn interactions, generate future frames, and support video reasoning with improved memory efficiency.

paragraphs: Imitation learning trains a policy from recorded expert behavior. When a single observation does not reveal the full situation, a policy needs observation history. Yet prior results have sometimes found that policies using only the latest observation perform better. This paper tackles that tension in visual imitation, where earlier proposed remedies had struggled to scale.

The approach gives additional training weight to demonstration keyframes at which the expert's action changes. This places greater emphasis on moments marking a change in behavior. The method is simple enough to apply to complex visual inputs, making action changepoints a practical source of structure in demonstration data.

Experiments report consistent improvements over all tested baselines on image-based Gym MuJoCo continuous-control tasks. In the CARLA urban-driving simulator, the method also demonstrates effective imitation using observation histories, addressing a longstanding behavioral-cloning issue described by the authors. These results support selective weighting of demonstration moments as a scalable way to improve learning from visual histories.
icml-2021-keyframe-focused-visual-imitat.tldr: Giving extra weight to expert action-change keyframes improves visual imitation and enables effective use of observation histories in simulated driving.

paragraphs: Speech carries information about delivery as well as speaker identity. This paper learns prosody representations directly from audio while seeking to reduce identifying timbral information. It uses a contrastive self-supervised signal and inductive biases based on the natural structure of prosody to separate prosodic information from representations of the speaker.

The authors introduce DAMMP, a spoken-language-understanding benchmark. Despite strong input downsampling and no access to linguistic information, their model performs comparably to state-of-the-art speech representations on this benchmark. This provides evidence that the retained prosodic information can remain useful even as the representation reduces other information available in the audio.

Minimum description length probing indicates that the representations selectively capture components of non-timbral prosody. The authors also find that their product quantizer separates these components without bottlenecks. Finally, they formulate speech de-identifiability in information-theoretic terms and use it to show lower identifiability than other speech representations. The stated result is a comparative reduction in identifiability, rather than a claim that identity information is entirely absent.
icml-2021-learning-de-identified-represe.tldr: A contrastive audio model learns useful prosody representations that retain less speaker-identifying information than other speech representations.

paragraphs: Neural network training can uncover regions containing multiple accurate but diverse solutions. Earlier methods for finding paths through such solutions required several training runs. This paper develops a single-run method that learns entire lines, curves, and simplexes of high-accuracy networks, at computational cost similar to training one model.

The learned subspace provides multiple solutions that can be combined into an ensemble. Reported ensemble performance approaches that of independently trained networks without requiring their separate training runs. The significance is that useful predictive diversity can be obtained within one training procedure, making a family of models available from a shared optimization process.

The subspace also offers a useful individual model at its midpoint. The authors report improvements in accuracy, calibration, and robustness to noisy labels, outperforming Stochastic Weight Averaging. These results connect two properties of the optimization landscape: diverse accurate solutions and wider minima associated with better performance. The method aims to benefit from both within the same training run.
icml-2021-learning-neural-network-subspa.tldr: One training run learns a subspace of accurate networks, enabling useful ensembles and improved midpoint models at roughly single-model training cost.

paragraphs: Inductive program synthesis constructs programs from examples of the behavior they should exhibit. Its success depends on having useful reusable functions and an effective strategy for searching combinations of those functions. This paper uses natural language annotations to guide the learning of both ingredients, linking descriptions of tasks with the structure of the synthesis system.

The proposed technique, LAPS, jointly guides library learning and neural search models. A better library supplies stronger building blocks, while a better search model helps find programs that solve a task. The authors integrate this approach into DreamCoder, an existing library-learning system, so that language can shape both what programs are built from and how they are discovered.

Evaluations cover string editing, image composition, and abstract reasoning about scenes. LAPS produces higher-quality libraries and improves search efficiency and generalization across these domains. These benefits persist when natural language hints are unavailable at test time, indicating that annotations can improve the learned synthesis machinery beyond the tasks where language is directly supplied.
icml-2021-leveraging-language-to-learn-p.tldr: LAPS uses language annotations to improve program libraries and search, with benefits that persist even without language hints at test time.

paragraphs: A neural network can make accurate predictions while leaving people with little insight into why it made a particular decision. This paper investigates a way to make those decisions easier to inspect: fit sparse linear models on top of feature representations learned by a deep network. Sparsity makes fewer learned features contribute to the linear prediction.

The resulting explanations provide a more compact account of how the learned representation supports a decision. The paper reports that these networks remain highly accurate while becoming more amenable to human interpretation. It supports that claim with both quantitative evaluation and human experiments, connecting the model design to people's ability to understand its behavior.

The authors demonstrate debugging uses in vision and language tasks. Sparse explanations help identify misleading correlations, explain incorrect classifications, and diagnose model biases. The contribution is therefore about making learned predictions easier to investigate: the explanations can reveal problematic behavior and support diagnosis, while preserving high predictive accuracy in the reported evaluations.
icml-2021-leveraging-sparse-linear-layer.tldr: Sparse linear models over deep features preserve high accuracy while making predictions easier to interpret and debug.

paragraphs: An inductive bias encourages a model to learn certain kinds of patterns or solutions. This paper hypothesizes that transformers can acquire useful reasoning biases from suitable generic training tasks. It develops LIME, a pretraining method that encodes these biases in synthetic datasets, shifting the design effort toward the tasks used to prepare the model.

The authors construct three tasks intended to require deduction, induction, and abduction. They deliberately exclude mathematical knowledge from these tasks so that pretraining targets fundamental reasoning tendencies rather than mathematical subject matter. This design tests whether preparation on abstract reasoning primitives can benefit later mathematical learning.

Models pretrained with LIME significantly outperform vanilla transformers on four different large mathematical reasoning benchmarks. The pretraining requires only a small fraction of the computation typically spent on the downstream task. These findings support the practical value of the proposed synthetic preparation and the hypothesis that suitable datasets can teach useful biases, without establishing that the tasks universally confer the three reasoning abilities.
icml-2021-lime-learning-inductive-bias-f.tldr: LIME uses inexpensive synthetic reasoning pretraining to improve transformer performance on four mathematical reasoning benchmarks.

paragraphs: Reviewer bidding helps conferences match papers with reviewers, but it also creates opportunities to manipulate assignments. A dishonest reviewer may bid on a collaborator's paper despite lacking relevant expertise, hoping to influence its acceptance. This paper studies the effectiveness of such attacks and finds that they can threaten the integrity of the reviewing process.

The authors develop a new bidding and assignment approach designed to be more robust against manipulation. Their evaluation includes demanding adversarial conditions: dishonest reviewers may coordinate, know how the assignment system works internally, and access its inputs. The reported robustness is empirical and explicitly includes these informed, colluding attackers.

The approach also produces assignment quality comparable to current methods that lack this robustness. This matters because protecting assignments is useful only alongside the ability to match papers and reviewers effectively. The results indicate that stronger resistance to bid manipulation can coexist with comparable assignment quality, providing evidence for improving the assignment mechanism itself as a defense.
icml-2021-making-paper-reviewing-robust-.tldr: A new reviewer bidding and assignment method empirically resists informed, colluding attackers while maintaining comparable assignment quality.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter optimization often uses a surrogate model to predict how well a proposed configuration will perform. Those predictions help decide which configuration to try next. When each trial is expensive, the surrogate must make useful choices from very little new evidence. This paper asks how experience from other datasets can improve that process.

Transfer NeuralProcesses, or TNP, is an end-to-end surrogate that learns from historical optimization work. It brings together parameters from earlier surrogates, previous trial results, and initial configurations used on other datasets. The motivating analogy is an expert who begins with settings that worked well before, but the proposed system learns how to transfer that experience.

Experiments use extensive OpenML datasets and three computer vision datasets. The authors report state-of-the-art performance with at least an order of magnitude fewer trials. The finding concerns trial efficiency in these evaluations: historical optimization knowledge can substantially reduce how many costly configurations need to be tested while still obtaining strong results.
icml-2021-meta-learning-hyperparameter-p.tldr: TNP transfers hyperparameter-search experience across datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance with at least an order of magnitude fewer trials in reported experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning when an adversary can corrupt some episodes of interaction. The initial setting is an episodic tabular Markov decision process, with a finite set of states and actions. The proposed algorithm, Corruption Robust Monotonic Value Propagation, assumes that the total number of corrupted episodes is known.

Its regret bound combines terms scaling as the square root of SAK, S squared times A, and CSA, with additional logarithmic factors, including polylogarithmic dependence on the planning horizon. Here S and A count states and actions, K counts episodes, and C measures corruption. A corresponding lower bound indicates that the upper bound is tight, giving theoretical context for the cost of learning under corruption.

The authors then apply their work to block MDPs, a setting involving rich observations. They provide what they identify as the first computationally efficient algorithm achieving square-root-in-K-type regret there. The contribution therefore includes both a corruption-robust learning guarantee and an application to efficient learning from richer observations.
icml-2021-on-reinforcement-learning-with.tldr: CR-MVP provides tight regret guarantees with a known corruption count, and the work yields efficient square-root-type regret for block MDPs.

paragraphs: Models of network spreading describe processes such as information propagation and diffusion. This paper focuses on learning a model whose predictions are accurate enough to support later optimization and control. The difficult setting is partial observation: only limited information about when network nodes become active is available, making standard likelihood-based learning quickly intractable on large networks.

The authors introduce a computationally efficient algorithm based on scalable dynamic message passing. It learns the parameters of an effective spreading model from the available activation-time information. The Independent Cascade model illustrates the approach, with the emphasis placed on the predictions obtainable through tractable inference.

The paper shows that tractable inference using the learned model predicts marginal probabilities better than using the original model. This highlights the value of learning parameters for the prediction procedure that will actually be used. A systematic method for learning mixtures of models further improves prediction quality, extending the same prediction-centered approach beyond a single effective model.
icml-2021-prediction-centric-learning-of.tldr: A dynamic message-passing method learns effective spreading models from partial observations to improve tractable predictions of network activation probabilities.

paragraphs: Image inverse problems reconstruct an image from measurements that may be incomplete, transformed, or noisy. This paper uses a normalizing flow prior to describe plausible images and formulates reconstruction as maximum a posteriori estimation. The chosen image is the one favored by the resulting probability model after conditioning on the measurements.

The formulation accommodates noise models with arbitrary dependencies and forward operators that can be nonlinear. These capabilities matter when measurement errors have structure or when the measurement process does more than apply a linear transformation. They allow the reconstruction objective to account for a broader range of observation processes within the same probabilistic framework.

The authors empirically validate the method on several inverse problems, including compressed sensing with quantized measurements and denoising with highly structured noise. These examples exercise the framework's ability to handle complicated measurement and noise behavior. The paper also provides initial theoretical recovery guarantees for inverse problems using a flow prior, complementing the experimental evidence with an early theoretical analysis.
icml-2021-solving-inverse-problems-with-.tldr: A flow-prior reconstruction framework handles dependent noise and nonlinear measurements, with empirical validation and initial recovery guarantees.

paragraphs: Sequence-learning problems often come with related tasks that differ in timing. A translation system can work with different amounts of input before producing output, while a forecasting model can predict different future days. These auxiliary tasks share temporal structure with the main task, creating opportunities for them to help train the same model.

The paper introduces a learnable scheduler that decides which auxiliary tasks to use during training. Its choices depend on the model's current state and the training data currently being processed. The scheduler and main-task model are trained jointly through bi-level optimization, allowing auxiliary-task selection to adapt as learning progresses.

Experiments show significant improvements in simultaneous machine translation and stock trend forecasting. The contribution is a mechanism for deciding when related tasks are useful, beyond simply recognizing that they exist. The reported findings support adaptive selection as a way to turn temporal relationships among tasks into better main-task performance in these two sequence-learning applications.
icml-2021-temporally-correlated-task-sch.tldr: A jointly trained scheduler adaptively selects temporally related auxiliary tasks, improving translation and stock-trend forecasting in experiments.

paragraphs: Understanding an architecture is easier when it has a clear computational model. This paper proposes such a model for transformer encoders through RASP, the Restricted Access Sequence Processing Language. It translates attention and feed-forward computation into simple programming primitives, providing a language for expressing algorithms that correspond to transformer-style computation.

The authors write RASP programs for histograms, sorting, and Dyck-language tasks. They also show how a transformer can be trained to imitate a RASP solution. These examples connect explicit programs with tasks a transformer could conceivably learn, making the architecture's operations easier to reason about at an algorithmic level.

Analyzing a RASP program gives an upper bound on the attention heads and layers needed to encode its task in a transformer. This describes sufficient architectural resources, rather than proving that fewer could never work. The authors further explore how this abstraction might explain phenomena reported in other work, presenting RASP as both a programming tool and a framework for architectural reasoning.
icml-2021-thinking-like-transformers-6d7.tldr: RASP expresses transformer-encoder computations as programs and yields upper bounds on the heads and layers needed to encode their tasks.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning learns representations by comparing related and contrasting examples, but explaining which features it learns requires examining the learning process. This paper studies a setting where data contain desired sparse features and unwanted dense features. The theoretical question is whether training can select the useful sparse structure while discarding the dense structure.

For ReLU networks, the authors prove that contrastive learning learns the desired features when appropriate augmentations are used. They explain this through feature decoupling: augmentations can weaken correlations in dense features between positive samples while preserving correlations in sparse features. The shared sparse structure then supplies the self-supervised signal that directs learning.

Empirical investigations find that this feature-decoupling principle matches the mechanism observed in practice. The result gives augmentations a specific explanatory role in determining what the representation retains. Its theoretical guarantee depends on the studied feature setting and suitable augmentations, while the experiments support the relevance of that explanation to practical contrastive learning.
icml-2021-toward-understanding-the-featu.tldr: Under the studied sparse-and-dense feature setting, suitable augmentations make contrastive ReLU networks learn desired features through feature decoupling.

paragraphs: Matrix-factorization recommenders represent users and items with latent factors learned from observed ratings. Their user-specific factors are learned transductively, making it difficult to accommodate newly arriving users immediately. This paper develops an inductive collaborative-filtering framework that can compute representations for query users through relationships with a group of key users.

The framework contains two representation models. The first factorizes the key users' rating matrix to obtain shared meta latents. The second uses attention-based structure learning to estimate hidden relationships between query users and key users. Neural message passing then uses those relationships and meta latents to compute embeddings for the query users.

The authors establish that the framework retains representation capacity equivalent to matrix factorization while enabling inductive user representations. Experiments report promising recommendations for users with few training ratings and for previously unseen users. These findings address two common open-world situations, showing how learned relationships to existing users can support representation construction as the user population expands.
icml-2021-towards-open-world-recommendat.tldr: An inductive recommender builds user embeddings through learned relationships to key users while retaining matrix factorization's representation capacity.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning trains policies from a fixed dataset, without collecting new experience through exploration. A major difficulty arises when learning updates bootstrap from states or actions outside that dataset's distribution. The paper hypothesizes that inadequate treatment of uncertainty helps explain why existing Q-learning and actor-critic methods can fail in this setting.

Uncertainty Weighted Actor-Critic, or UWAC, identifies out-of-distribution state-action pairs and reduces their contribution to training objectives. It estimates uncertainty with dropout, using a practical procedure that adds little overhead to existing reinforcement-learning algorithms. Uncertainty therefore affects how strongly particular training signals influence learning.

Experiments show substantially improved training stability and performance exceeding existing offline methods on a variety of competitive tasks. The authors report especially significant gains over the state-of-the-art baseline on datasets containing sparse human-expert demonstrations. These results support uncertainty-based weighting as a practical response to unreliable learning signals when the available experience is fixed and provides limited coverage.
icml-2021-uncertainty-weighted-actor-cri.tldr: UWAC uses dropout-based uncertainty to down-weight out-of-distribution training signals, improving offline reinforcement-learning stability and performance in experiments.

paragraphs: The best balance between transformer depth and width can vary substantially across data types. This paper investigates an explanation rooted in the input representation: vocabulary size and embedding rank. It theoretically predicts a bottleneck in which embedding rank limits how much additional self-attention width can contribute to the model's expressivity.

Under this account, a small vocabulary or low embedding rank gives depth an additional advantage over width. The authors empirically demonstrate the bottleneck and its consequences for architecture design. Their analysis links cross-domain differences in preferred transformer shapes to differences in vocabulary sizes and embedding ranks that might otherwise receive little attention.

The framework also identifies size redundancies of 25%–50% in leading language models including ALBERT and T5. This result concerns redundancies revealed by the rank-based analysis. More broadly, the work argues that architecture choices should account for the information capacity of the input embedding, since wider attention layers may encounter a representational constraint imposed earlier in the model.
icml-2021-which-transformer-architecture.tldr: An embedding-rank bottleneck links vocabulary properties to transformer depth–width choices and reveals substantial size redundancies in studied language models.
